lesson.title: Counting the Bonds: What Bond Order Tells You
lesson.summary: Bond order is the number of shared electron pairs between two bonded atoms, and it is one of the best predictors of how strong and how short that bond will be.
lesson.body:
Bond order is simply the number of bonding pairs shared between two specific atoms in a structure: a single bond has a bond order of 1, a double bond has a bond order of 2, and a triple bond has a bond order of 3. It is a direct extension of everything you already know about single, double, and triple bonds, just expressed as a single number that makes bonds easy to compare across different molecules.

Nitrogen gas, N2, with its triple bond, has a bond order of 3 between the two nitrogens, the highest common bond order for a simple diatomic molecule and part of why N2 is so famously unreactive. Oxygen gas, O2, has a Lewis structure with one O=O double bond, giving a bond order of 2, though a full molecular orbital treatment refines this simple picture and explains oxygen's magnetic behavior, a topic for more advanced study. Hydrogen gas, H2, with its single shared pair, has a bond order of just 1. Carbon monoxide, CO, the molecule from the triple bonds section, has a bond order of 3 as well, its carbon and oxygen atoms are connected by three shared pairs even though the two elements are different, a reminder that bond order depends only on how many pairs are shared, not on which two elements are doing the sharing.

Bond order does not have to be a whole number. When a real molecule is a resonance hybrid, its bond order is the average of the bond orders across all contributing resonance structures. Ozone, O3, is the example you have already worked through: one resonance structure has an O=O double bond, order 2, next to an O-O single bond, order 1, and the other resonance structure swaps them. Averaging the two structures for either O-O bond gives 2 plus 1, divided by 2, equals 1.5, matching the fact that ozone's two oxygen-oxygen bonds are experimentally identical and intermediate in length between a single and a double bond.

The same averaging applies to carbonate and nitrate. Nitrate has three resonance structures, each with one N=O double bond, order 2, and two N-O single bonds, order 1, at any given moment. Averaged across all three equivalent structures, every nitrogen oxygen bond works out to a bond order of 2 plus 1 plus 1, divided by 3, equals about 1.33. This fractional bond order is not a rounding error, it is a real, measurable property of the molecule, reflected in nitrate's uniformly shortened and strengthened N-O bonds compared to a hypothetical pure N-O single bond.

Bond order matters because it predicts real physical properties directly: higher bond order generally means a shorter, stronger bond, and lower bond order means a longer, weaker one, holding the bonded elements constant. This relationship, covered in full in the next section on bond length, is one of the most reliable trends in Lewis structure chemistry, and it is exactly why chemists bother counting bonding pairs so carefully in the first place, since that count predicts something you can actually measure in the lab.
